To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the continental shelf of eastern Canada and the United States is probably not a product of isostatic depression of the basement beneath the sedimentary fill, but is due partly to sinking of the basement beneath a sedimentary trough.

the Atlantic Continental Shelf was formed by a combination of isostatic sinking, crustal thinning by subcrustal currents, and differential depression of the continental crust beneath the sediment load.
the continental shelf of the Atlantic coastal plain is a sedimentary feature that is in part the result of the sinking of the crust beneath the sediment load supplied by the coastal rivers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the Atlantic Coastal Plain and its offshore extension, the Continental Shelf.
the evolution of the continental margin, and the results are based on the assumption of an essentially horizontal basement prior to sedimentation.
the evolution of the continental shelf and its relation to the history of the Atlantic Ocean.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the sedimentary trough was formed in part at least by isostatic downwarp of the crust beneath the sediment load supplied by the streams and in part by differential sinking of the crust due to subcrustal erosional currents.
the Atlantic Shelf has been formed by a combination of sedimentation and crustal thinning, and that the latter is due to subcrustal currents and erosion.
the continental shelf was formed by isostatic depression of a crust that had thinned by subcrustal currents, and that the basins and the ridge were produced by instabilities of the thin crust.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the sedimentary trough is a result of isostatic sinking beneath a sediment load, but the sinking is due to subcrustal currents which have eroded the crust beneath the M discontinuous and thus permitted the crust to subside.

the Atlantic continental shelf has been formed largely by erosion, that the rate of erosion has been roughly constant for the last 200 million years, and that erosion of the basement has produced the sedimentary trough and the median ridge.
the Atlantic Coastal Plain and the Continental Shelf are the result of erosion, isostatic sinking, and subcrustal thinning of the continental crust.

the Atlantic continental margin is an excellent natural laboratory for studying the interaction between tectonic processes and sedimentation in a forearc environment.
the Atlantic continental shelf is a dynamic system, not just a passive sediment trap.
